caption: Pielou's evenness per study and host species, split by developmental stage, after rarefying every sample to 1000 reads. Boxes are per-study quartiles; the vertical line in each panel is the median for that species at that stage, absent where the stage was not sampled. The x axis is shared by both stages. Rows are grouped by plant family, families ordered by ascending median evenness and species by ascending median within each family. Samples below the depth are excluded rather than rarefied, as are samples with a single ASV, for which evenness is undefined. The table lists each contributing study with its accession, samples, species and median evenness.

Alpha diversity in seeds and seedlings after rarefying every sample to the same depth (columns), for observed ASV richness, Shannon and Pielou's evenness (rows). Boxes show the median and interquartile range, whiskers 1.5 times the interquartile range, points outliers. Each panel gives the Kruskal-Wallis test of developmental stage across all studies pooled, with its H-based effect size; samples below a depth are excluded at that depth, so sample numbers differ between columns. Study is not controlled for in these pooled tests; per-study tests are in alpha_diversity_findings.csv.

As for the plant-family alluvial, but resolved to host species and grouped by plant family. Only species with a study sampling both stages are shown, so the panel set is smaller than the full species list. Supplementary to the family-level version.

Genus composition at each developmental stage, by plant family. Only studies that sampled both seeds and seedlings of that family contribute, so both bars rest on the same studies (n in each strip); relative abundance is averaged within each study, then across studies, so every study counts equally. Ribbon width is the mean relative abundance of a genus; each stage sums to 100%. Ribbons link the same genus name across stages and do NOT indicate that cells persisted, were inherited or were transmitted - seeds and seedlings are different, unpaired samples. The 15 genera most abundant across all studies are named, with the same colours in every genus figure, and all others pooled as Other.

Change in genus relative abundance from seed to seedling within each host species, for the 15 genera named in the alluvial figures. Colour is log2(seedling / seed) of the study-averaged relative abundances, from the same studies that sampled both stages, with a pseudocount of 1e-4 added to both; values beyond +/-6 are capped, and ratios where one stage is near zero mostly reflect the pseudocount. Dot size is the larger of the two stage means.

Dendrogram of every bacterial ASV that passed filtering, pruned from the phylogenetic tree of all ASVs and midpoint-rooted; branch lengths are not drawn and tips are not labelled. Tip points are coloured by phylum, the seven phyla with the most ASVs named and the rest grouped as Other. The rings, from the centre outwards, give each ASV's genus (the eleven genera with the most ASVs named, the rest grey) and its prevalence in seeds and in seedlings, as the percentage of that stage's samples in which the ASV was detected, on a shared square-root colour scale, from near-white to that stage's colour. All studies are pooled.

Dendrogram of the most prevalent bacterial ASVs, those detected in at least 50% of the samples of at least one study; no ASV reaches 50% of all samples pooled. The tree is pruned from the phylogenetic tree of all ASVs and midpoint-rooted; branch lengths are not drawn. Rings, from the centre outwards, give each ASV's phylum, its genus (the eleven genera with the most ASVs named, the rest grouped), and its prevalence in seeds and in seedlings as the percentage of all samples of that stage in which it was detected.

Dendrogram of the 50 most abundant bacterial genera, pruned from the phylogenetic tree of all ASVs to one tip per genus (its most abundant ASV) and midpoint-rooted; branch lengths are not drawn. Tip points are coloured by phylum. The inner ring gives each genus's mean relative abundance in seeds and the outer ring in seedlings, as the mean of per-sample relative abundances on a shared square-root colour scale, from near-white to that stage's colour. Compound SILVA genus names are shortened to their first name followed by 'group'. All studies are pooled, so the rings are dominated by the largest study.
